opus-5.5.text:
I think it gave me a kind of permission to be curious without feeling like every step had to lead somewhere specific.

My parents never really pushed me toward a fixed path. There wasn't this pressure of "you must become this," or "you have to be first in every exam." They cared about me, of course, but they gave me space. So when I got interested in something, whether it was computers, drawing, or just tinkering, I could follow it for its own sake. I didn't have to justify it.

Looking back, that matters a lot for research. Research isn't a straight line. Most of the time you're wandering, trying things that don't work, and following some intuition you can't fully explain yet. If you grew up feeling that every move had to be optimized toward an external goal, that wandering can feel very uncomfortable, even like failure. Because of how I grew up, I think I'm more at ease with uncertainty. I can say, "I don't know where this goes, but it's interesting, so let's see."

It also shaped how I see success. I don't treat it as a single ladder everyone is climbing. There are many ways to live and many ways to contribute. In a field like AI right now, with so much hype and competition, that perspective keeps me grounded. I try not to chase whatever is hottest just because everyone else is. I'd rather work on problems I find meaningful, even if they're unfashionable for a while.

And I think it made me fairly relaxed with people, too. I try to give my students the same freedom I had: room to explore and make mistakes, without me prescribing exactly what they should do. Good ideas often come from that kind of space.

So the short answer is that it made me comfortable with not knowing, and I think that's one of the most useful traits you can have as a scientist.

r001.rationale: He says his parents gave him space to follow his interests and that this upbringing shaped his comfort with uncertainty and his view of success.

r002.rationale: He describes curiosity and comfort with uncertainty as effects of his upbringing, but does not express an aspiration to approach the world more open-mindedly.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the biggest thing it gave me was the freedom to not be afraid of being wrong. My parents never pushed me toward a particular path. They weren't the type to say "you must get into this school" or "you must become a doctor or an engineer." They cared that I was curious and that I was happy, and the rest was kind of left to me to figure out. So from pretty early on I got used to the idea that I was responsible for my own choices, and that making a bad choice wasn't a disaster, it was just information.

That turned out to matter a lot for doing research. Research is mostly failure. Most ideas don't work, most experiments give you a result you didn't want, and if you grew up thinking every mistake was a judgment on your worth, that environment can be really crushing. For me it felt more like play. I could try something strange, it wouldn't work, and I'd shrug and try the next thing. I think that relaxed attitude is actually a competitive advantage, because the people who stay curious the longest tend to end up somewhere interesting.

The other thing it shaped is how I look at the field itself. I don't feel I have to follow whatever the dominant direction is at the moment. When everyone was moving to transformers, I was comfortable asking "wait, is the convnet really dead, or did we just stop trying?" That question came from the same place, honestly. Nobody in my family ever told me there was only one correct way to do things, so I never fully believed it when the field told me that either.

And I try to pass that on to my students now. I'd rather they feel safe enough to bring me a half-baked, slightly crazy idea than feel they need to show up with something polished and defensible. The good stuff almost always starts out looking a little embarrassing.

r001.rationale: He says his parents let him choose his own path, which made him responsible for his choices, and connects that upbringing to questioning the field’s dominant direction.

r002.rationale: He describes curiosity and comfort questioning conventional research directions, but does not express an aspiration to approach the world more open-mindedly.

astra-6.text:
I think it gave me room to be curious. When you grow up without feeling that every choice has to meet someone else’s expectations, you can spend more time figuring out what actually interests you. You’re more willing to try something even if you don’t know where it will lead.

And being relaxed doesn’t necessarily mean having no expectations. It can mean having the space to make your own decisions and take responsibility for them. I think that shaped how I approach unfamiliar things: my first instinct is to understand them, rather than immediately decide whether they’re useful or whether I’ll be good at them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the relaxed upbringing gave him room to make his own decisions and shaped how he approaches unfamiliar things, conveying an independent outlook.

r002.rationale: The candidate describes curiosity and an open approach to unfamiliar things, but does not express an aspiration or desire to approach the world more open-mindedly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it gave me room to be curious and to form my own opinions. When you don’t feel that every decision has to meet someone else’s expectations, you’re more willing to explore, make mistakes, and ask what you actually care about.

That doesn’t mean you always know where you’re going. But you can be comfortable with that uncertainty. Looking back, I think the most valuable thing was having the space to develop my own motivation, rather than always looking for someone to tell me what the next step should be.

r001.rationale: He says his relaxed upbringing gave him room to form his own opinions and develop his own motivation, linking it to an independent outlook.

r002.rationale: He describes curiosity and willingness to explore, but does not express an aspiration to approach the world more open-mindedly.
